blood-test-preparation-and-fasting.name: Preparing for a blood test: fasting explained
blood-test-preparation-and-fasting.summary: Some blood tests need fasting or a change to what you eat, drink or take beforehand; the person who arranges the test should say which applies.
keyPoints: Whether a blood test needs preparation depends on the test, and the clinician who arranges it should say what applies.
For some tests the preparation is a period without food or drink other than water, and the person arranging the test will say if anything else applies.
Food and drink can change some results because nutrients from a meal may still be in the blood at the time of the test.
Results usually reach the GP or hospital team, and timing varies from a few days to a few weeks depending on the test.

body.heading: Does every blood test need preparation?
body.body:
Whether a blood test needs preparation depends on the type of test. The NHS says the healthcare professional arranging the test will tell you if you need to prepare.

For some tests, preparation means not eating or drinking anything other than water for a set time beforehand.

body.heading: Why does fasting matter?
body.body:
Fasting means going without food and drink, apart from water, for a period before the test. The reason is that nutrients from food enter the bloodstream and may still be there when the sample is taken, which can change the results of some blood tests.

The length of the fast depends on the test being done. NHS hospital leaflets give different lengths for different tests, so the person arranging the test can say which applies.

body.heading: What counts as water only, and what about medicines?
body.body:
Practices that publish fasting advice usually mean water only. Tea, coffee, including black coffee, and sugar-free drinks are not counted as water, and some practices also list vaping and nicotine patches.

People are advised not to change their medicines unless a doctor has told them to. People with diabetes are advised to check with their doctor before fasting for a test.

body.heading: What if I did not fast, or I am not sure?
body.body: If you are not sure whether fasting applies, the practice or clinic can tell you. A test can still go ahead without fasting, but the doctor may ask for a repeat test after fasting if the result needs it.

body.heading: What happens to the sample, and when do results come back?
body.body:
Timing varies. Some results are ready within a few days, and others take a few weeks. Results go to the GP or the hospital team that arranged the test, and some people can also see them in the NHS App.

The NHS advises contacting the GP surgery or specialist if you have not heard anything after a few weeks. A GP appointment is the route for questions about what a result means.

psa-test-what-it-shows-and-what-the-nhs-.name: PSA test: what it shows and what the NHS says
psa-test-what-it-shows-and-what-the-nhs-.summary: A PSA test measures prostate-specific antigen in the blood. The NHS says it is not a routine screening test, and results can be wrong in both directions.
keyPoints: A PSA test is a blood test that measures prostate-specific antigen, and a high level may be a sign of a prostate condition.
The NHS does not offer routine PSA screening, though testing is offered to some people, including men with a faulty BRCA2 gene and those with symptoms that suggest prostate cancer.
Men aged 50 or over without symptoms can ask their GP about a PSA test, after discussing the benefits and risks.
PSA results can be falsely reassuring or falsely alarming, and the test can find slow-growing cancers that might never have caused harm.

body.heading: What is a PSA test?
body.body:
A PSA test is a blood test that measures the amount of prostate-specific antigen. Prostate Cancer UK says a raised PSA may suggest a prostate problem, but not necessarily cancer.

A raised PSA can have several causes, so it is not a diagnosis on its own.

body.heading: Is PSA testing part of NHS screening?
body.body:
No. The NHS says routine PSA testing is not currently offered. The exception it describes is for men whose genetic tests have shown a faulty version of a gene called BRCA2.

A PSA test may also be recommended when someone has symptoms that could point to prostate cancer.

body.heading: Can I ask my GP for a PSA test?
body.body:
Outside the groups above, the NHS describes an informed-choice route in which a person can ask a GP about PSA testing. Men aged 50 or over can ask their GP about PSA testing even without symptoms.

The aim is to give clear information on the advantages and disadvantages of the test first. Asking a GP is the route to start that conversation.

body.heading: What are the benefits of a PSA test?
body.body: A GOV.UK programme page, now withdrawn, said a large European trial showed PSA testing can reduce the risk of death from prostate cancer.

body.heading: What are the limits and risks?
body.body:
The NHS says PSA tests are unreliable. A result can suggest cancer when there is none, which is called a false positive. A normal result does not rule cancer out either: the NHS says around 1 in 7 men with a normal PSA may have prostate cancer.

The test can also find cancers that are unlikely to cause harm, known as overdiagnosis. Overtreatment of such cancers is a recognised concern. This is why the NHS presents the decision as an informed choice.

Anyone worried about symptoms can contact a GP; NHS 111 can advise if the surgery is closed, and 999 is for emergencies.

lumbar-puncture-what-happens-and-what-to.name: Lumbar puncture: what happens and what to expect
lumbar-puncture-what-happens-and-what-to.summary: A lumbar puncture uses a needle in the lower back to collect the fluid around the spinal cord, and the pressure of the fluid may also be measured.
keyPoints: A lumbar puncture is usually done in hospital under local anaesthetic, and leaflets give different times, from about 15 minutes to 40 minutes.
Fluid from around the spinal cord is collected for testing.
A headache is the most common side effect, and serious complications are described as extremely rare.
Some results come back within a day and others take weeks, so the team can say when to expect them.

body.heading: What is a lumbar puncture?
body.body:
A lumbar puncture is a procedure in which a needle is placed between the bones of the lower spine to reach the fluid that surrounds the spinal cord and brain. This fluid is called cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF.

The NHS says it is usually done in hospital. A local anaesthetic numbs the lower back, the needle goes in between the spinal bones and fluid is collected for testing.

Doctors use it to collect spinal fluid for testing and to measure the pressure of the fluid.

body.heading: What happens during the procedure?
body.body:
One leaflet says it typically takes around 15 to 20 minutes but can take longer, and another says 20 to 40 minutes. The lower back is cleaned and numbed with a local anaesthetic injection before the needle is placed.

Leaflets say to expect to rest flat for a short period afterwards, and the team caring for you gives the details.

body.heading: What are the side effects and risks?
body.body:
Headache, back pain and bruising are common side effects. The headache is the most frequent. It can start from a few hours to two days after the procedure and last for a few days.

Leaflets say lying flat usually helps the headache.

Serious complications are described as extremely rare. Very rare complications include infection, bleeding, nerve injury, hearing loss and double vision. One hospital trust leaflet says serious harm from complications like these occurs in fewer than one in 10,000 lumbar punctures.

body.heading: When should I get help after a lumbar puncture?
body.body: Leaflets list a severe headache that does not ease on lying flat, a fever, neck stiffness or leg weakness as reasons to get urgent advice from the hospital team or NHS 111. The hospital team who did the test, NHS 111 or the GP the same day can advise, and 999 is for emergencies.

body.heading: When do results come back?
body.body: It depends on the test. Some results can come back within a day. Other tests take longer, sometimes up to 10 weeks. The team caring for you can say when to expect them.

cystoscopy-what-happens-and-what-to-expe.name: Cystoscopy: what happens and what to expect
cystoscopy-what-happens-and-what-to-expe.summary: A cystoscopy uses a thin camera passed through the urethra to look inside the bladder. It can be flexible, usually with local anaesthetic gel, or rigid, usually under general or spinal anaesthetic.
keyPoints: A cystoscopy looks inside the bladder through the urethra using a thin tube with a camera.
A flexible cystoscopy is usually done under local anaesthetic, and a rigid one under general or spinal anaesthetic.
It can be used to check bladder symptoms, take small tissue samples or treat bladder conditions.
Mild burning and a little bleeding when passing urine are common and usually settle within a few days.

body.heading: What is a cystoscopy?
body.body:
A cystoscopy is a test that looks inside the bladder. A thin tube with a camera, called a cystoscope, is passed along the urethra, the tube that carries urine out of the body, and into the bladder.

NHS sources describe two types. A flexible cystoscopy uses a thin, bendable tube and is often used to check bladder symptoms. A rigid cystoscopy uses a straight tube that does not bend and is often used to treat bladder conditions. A cystoscopy can also let clinicians take biopsies, which are small pieces of tissue sent for testing.

body.heading: What anaesthetic is used?
body.body:
A flexible cystoscopy is usually done under local anaesthetic, with a numbing gel, and does not need a general anaesthetic.

A rigid cystoscopy is done under general anaesthetic, which means being asleep. A spinal anaesthetic is also possible. For this type, people are usually told not to eat or drink for several hours beforehand.

body.heading: What happens during a flexible cystoscopy?
body.body:
Local anaesthetic gel is applied first.

The cystoscope is then passed in. The bladder is filled with water, which can bring on a feeling of needing to pass urine. Men may find the passage past the prostate briefly uncomfortable.

body.heading: How soon can I go home, and what are the after-effects?
body.body:
Most flexible cystoscopies are day cases, and people can usually leave once they feel ready.

Common effects include mild burning when passing urine and a little bleeding, which usually settle within a few days. Leaflets suggest drinking extra fluids afterwards.

Less common problems include a urine infection and difficulty passing urine. After a rigid cystoscopy, narrowing of the urethra is a listed risk, and bleeding is more likely after a biopsy.

Leaflets say to contact a GP for severe pain, heavy bleeding, a fever or being unable to pass urine. NHS 111 can advise out of hours, and 999 is for emergencies.

nhs-screening-who-is-invited-and-how-oft.name: NHS screening: who is invited and how often
nhs-screening-who-is-invited-and-how-oft.summary: In England the NHS invites eligible people for bowel, breast, cervical, abdominal aortic aneurysm and diabetic eye screening. Who is invited depends on age, sex and health.
keyPoints: NHS screening in England invites people who have no symptoms, based on age, sex or health, rather than testing everyone.
Breast screening is offered every three years, and cervical screening every five years for eligible ages.
Bowel screening is offered every two years, and men are invited once for an abdominal aortic aneurysm scan in the year they turn 65.
People with diabetes aged 12 or over are invited for eye screening, and some people outside the usual ages can ask for screening themselves.

body.heading: What is screening for?
body.body:
Screening checks people who have no symptoms to find a condition or a risk of it earlier. The NHS programmes described here invite people automatically, based on their age, sex or health, using the details held by their GP.

Screening is separate from tests arranged for symptoms. Anyone with symptoms should see a GP rather than wait for a screening invitation.

body.heading: Who is invited for bowel screening?
body.body:
Bowel cancer screening is offered to adults in a set age range, with an upper age of 74, and invitations come every two years.

People aged 75 and over can ask for screening every two years by phoning the free bowel cancer screening helpline.

body.heading: Who is invited for breast and cervical screening?
body.body:
Women are offered breast screening every three years from the age of 50 up to their 71st birthday. Women over 71 can still be screened every three years by making their own appointment with their local breast screening unit.

Cervical screening is for women and people with a cervix aged 25 to 64. Since July 2025, people aged 25 to 64 are invited every five years.

body.heading: Who is invited for an aortic aneurysm scan?
body.body:
An abdominal aortic aneurysm is a swelling in the main blood vessel running through the abdomen. Screening is for men, who receive an invitation by post at the age of 64 or 65.

Men who have not been screened can contact their local screening service to arrange a test themselves.

body.heading: What about diabetic eye screening?
body.body:
People with diabetes aged 12 or over are invited for diabetic eye screening on a regular schedule. Invitations come every year, or every two years if the last two screens found no changes in the eyes.

The screening checks the back of the eye for changes caused by diabetes.

body.heading: What if I have not had an invitation?
body.body: A person who thinks they should have been invited, or who is outside the usual ages, can ask their GP surgery or the local screening service. A GP appointment is the usual route for any symptom, whatever the screening history, and NHS 111 can advise if the surgery is closed.

pregnancy-scans-and-tests-on-the-nhs.name: Pregnancy scans and tests on the NHS
pregnancy-scans-and-tests-on-the-nhs.summary: NHS pregnancy care includes booking blood tests, a dating scan and a mid-pregnancy anomaly scan, plus optional screening for Down's, Edwards' and Patau's syndromes.
keyPoints: The booking appointment with a midwife is usually between 8 and 12 weeks and includes blood tests and checks of blood pressure and urine.
The dating scan, usually at 11 to 14 weeks, estimates the due date from the baby's measurements.
Screening for Down's, Edwards' and Patau's syndromes is a choice, and taking part is up to the pregnant person.
The mid-pregnancy anomaly scan usually takes place between 18 and 21 weeks and checks for 11 physical conditions in the baby.

body.heading: What happens at the booking appointment?
body.body:
The booking appointment is the first main antenatal visit, and the NHS gives the usual timing as between 8 and 12 weeks. The midwife checks blood pressure and urine and offers a blood group test.

Blood is also taken at or around this time. NHS trusts describe booking-stage blood tests for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, sickle cell and thalassaemia, and the exact list can vary between trusts.

body.heading: What is the dating scan?
body.body: The dating scan is an ultrasound scan, usually offered at 11 to 14 weeks. It estimates when the baby is due from the baby's measurements.

body.heading: Is screening for Down's, Edwards' and Patau's syndromes compulsory?
body.body:
Taking part in this screening is a choice. If a person chooses it, the combined test pairs a blood test taken between 10 and 14 weeks with a measurement of the fluid at the back of the baby's neck, taken during the dating scan.

Edwards' and Patau's syndromes are also looked for at the mid-pregnancy scan if the person chooses screening. A blood test called the quad test, taken between 14 and 20 weeks, can be used for Down's syndrome when the combined test was not possible. It is less accurate than the combined test.

body.heading: What does the mid-pregnancy anomaly scan look at?
body.body:
The anomaly scan is an ultrasound that checks for 11 physical conditions in the baby and the position of the placenta, though not every condition can be found. The NHS lists it as usually between 18 and 21 weeks, and some trusts describe it as taking place between 20 and 22 weeks.

Screening for Edwards' and Patau's syndromes forms part of this scan for those who choose it.

body.heading: What if a screening result says there is a higher chance?
body.body:
A higher-chance result is not a diagnosis. The options described are a more accurate screening blood test, called the non-invasive prenatal test or NIPT, a diagnostic test such as chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, or no further tests.

The NHS summary says there are no known risks to the pregnant person or the baby from the blood tests or scans used for this screening. Diagnostic tests, such as chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, are different from screening and can give a definite answer. If the screening finds something, the person is contacted sooner.

For urgent concerns in pregnancy, the midwife, maternity unit or NHS 111 can advise, and 999 is for emergencies.

pet-and-bone-scans-what-to-expect.name: PET and bone scans: what to expect
pet-and-bone-scans-what-to-expect.summary: PET and bone scans both use a small amount of radioactive tracer given by injection. Both scans involve a waiting period after the injection.
keyPoints: A PET scan uses a small amount of radioactive tracer given by injection to scan inside the body.
PET scans help diagnose or plan treatment for conditions such as cancer, dementia and epilepsy.
A bone scan uses a tracer that collects in bone and shows areas where bone is breaking down and being repaired.
Both involve a small amount of radiation, and hospitals give their own instructions on preparation and waiting times.

body.heading: What is a PET scan?
body.body:
The NHS describes a PET scan as a test that uses a small amount of radiation to scan inside the body. A small amount of radioactive tracer is given by injection.

A PET-CT scan combines the PET scan with a CT scan.

body.heading: Why would I need one?
body.body: The NHS says PET scans are used to diagnose or plan treatment for certain conditions, such as cancer, dementia or epilepsy.

body.heading: What is a bone scan?
body.body:
A bone scan is a nuclear medicine test that looks at the activity of cells in the bones. A tracer is injected, collects in the bones, and a special camera takes pictures of it.

Areas where more tracer collects show up as hot spots. A bone scan can show areas where bone is breaking down and being repaired.

body.heading: How do I prepare, and what is the day like?
body.body:
Hospitals usually give fasting instructions for a PET scan, which vary, and ask people to remove metal items such as jewellery.

After the injection, people usually rest for around an hour while the tracer spreads through the body. The scan itself usually takes around 30 to 60 minutes, and longer at some hospitals, and people need to stay still.

For a bone scan, leaflets describe a wait of a few hours after the injection, and some suggest drinking plenty of fluids and emptying the bladder often. A camera then takes pictures of the bones.

Each hospital's own leaflet has the exact instructions.

body.heading: Is the radiation a concern?
body.body:
Both scans involve a small amount of radiation. The NHS describes the radiation risk from the tracer injection as very small. Hospital leaflets describe the radiation dose from a bone scan as small.

Some hospitals advise limiting close, prolonged contact with pregnant women and young children for a period afterwards, and staff say for how long. Departments ask anyone who is or might be pregnant to contact them before the scan.

body.heading: When do results come back?
body.body:
After a PET scan people can usually go home soon afterwards. A radiologist reviews the images and the report goes to the doctor who referred the person. The NHS says it usually takes 1 or 2 weeks to get PET scan results.

Bone scan results vary by hospital, from days to a few weeks, so the hospital that arranged the scan can say.

coronary-angiogram-what-happens-and-risk.name: Coronary angiogram: what happens and risks
coronary-angiogram-what-happens-and-risk.summary: A coronary angiogram is an X-ray test that uses dye to show narrowed or blocked heart arteries. It is done under local anaesthetic and most people go home the same day.
keyPoints: A coronary angiogram uses X-ray images and contrast dye to show narrowings or blockages in the arteries that supply the heart.
It is done under local anaesthetic, through an artery in the wrist or groin.
Bruising, soreness and a small lump near the entry site are common, and the risk of serious complications is very small.
If a blockage is found, treatment such as angioplasty with a stent can sometimes be done during the same procedure.

body.heading: What does a coronary angiogram show?
body.body:
A coronary angiogram is an X-ray of the coronary arteries, the blood vessels that supply the heart muscle. These arteries do not show on ordinary X-rays, so dye is used to make them visible.

It helps doctors look for narrowing, blockages and blood flow problems. It is also called cardiac catheterisation.

body.heading: What happens during the test?
body.body:
It is done under local anaesthetic. A thin tube called a catheter is passed in through the wrist or groin, and X-ray images guide it to the coronary arteries.

Contrast dye is injected while X-ray images are taken. The test usually takes between 30 minutes and 2 hours.

body.heading: Is it done through the wrist or the groin?
body.body:
The cardiologist chooses whether to use the wrist or the groin. The wrist is often used, and the choice affects aftercare.

Wrist access usually means faster recovery and fewer restrictions. With groin access people may need to lie flat for a period afterwards.

body.heading: What are the risks?
body.body:
The NHS describes the risk of serious complications as very small. Bruising and a collection of blood under the skin, called a haematoma, where the catheter went in are the most common problems.

A very small risk of more serious problems is listed, including an allergic reaction to the contrast dye, stroke or heart attack.

body.heading: What is recovery like?
body.body:
Most people go home the same day. A compression band is often placed on the wrist, or a seal or pressure device on the groin, to close the entry point. Bruising and soreness for a few days or weeks are common.

Leaflets list a growing or painful lump, swelling, redness, discharge, or a cold, pale or painful hand or leg as reasons to seek advice. The ward or the GP can advise, and NHS 111 can help out of hours.

Leaflets say bleeding from the entry site that does not stop with firm pressure needs a 999 call.

body.heading: What happens if a narrowing is found?
body.body:
The images show whether arteries are narrowed or blocked. If it is unclear how severe a narrowing is, doctors may measure pressure with a wire in the artery or scan it from inside with a tiny imaging device.

If a blockage is found, treatment such as angioplasty with a stent can sometimes be done at the same time.

blood-transfusion-why-and-how-it-is-done.name: Blood transfusion: why and how it is done
blood-transfusion-why-and-how-it-is-done.summary: A blood transfusion gives red blood cells, plasma or platelets from a donor to someone who has lost blood or has a condition affecting their blood. The NHS describes it as generally safe, though complications can rarely occur.
keyPoints: Transfusions are used after major blood loss and for conditions that affect the blood or bone marrow.
Blood is matched to the person's blood group first, because the wrong ABO group can be life-threatening.
The NHS describes transfusion as generally safe, with complications such as infection or an allergic reaction rare.
All blood donated in the UK is tested for infection by NHS Blood and Transplant.

body.heading: Why would someone need a blood transfusion?
body.body:
The NHS says a transfusion can help when a person has lost a lot of blood, or has a condition that affects the blood or bone marrow. Platelets or plasma may be given to treat or prevent bleeding.

In children, transfusions may replace blood lost during an operation or after an accident, or treat conditions such as severe anaemia, sickle cell disease or thalassaemia. Blood components such as platelets and plasma, which help blood to clot, can also be given.

body.heading: How is blood matched?
body.body:
A blood sample is taken before the transfusion to check that donor blood is the right blood group.

Giving blood from the wrong ABO group can be life-threatening, which is why the checks are strict. The Rh D group also matters: Rh D negative women who could become pregnant are normally given Rh D negative red cells, to avoid harmful antibodies.

body.heading: What happens during a transfusion?
body.body:
Blood transfusions take place in hospital. Blood or a blood component is usually given through a thin tube into a vein.

The hospital team can explain what to expect on the day.

body.heading: What are the risks and side effects?
body.body:
The NHS describes a blood transfusion as generally safe. Rarely, complications such as an infection or an allergic reaction can happen, and they can appear a few hours, days or even weeks later.

Some people have mild side effects, such as a raised temperature or a skin rash. Pulse, temperature and blood pressure are monitored during the transfusion. Anyone who feels unwell after going home can contact the hospital team, NHS 111 or a GP, and 999 is for emergencies.

body.heading: How safe is the blood supply?
body.body: All blood donated in the UK is tested for infection by NHS Blood and Transplant. Any donation that reacts in the initial tests is not used.

general-anaesthetic-before-during-and-af.name: General anaesthetic: before, during, after
general-anaesthetic-before-during-and-af.summary: A general anaesthetic puts a person into controlled unconsciousness for surgery. Preparation includes fasting, and common effects afterwards are sickness, shivering and a sore throat.
keyPoints: A general anaesthetic produces a state of controlled unconsciousness.
Fasting beforehand matters because food or liquid in the stomach could be breathed into the lungs.
Common effects afterwards include sickness, feeling cold or shivering, a sore throat and drowsiness.
Every general anaesthetic carries some risk, and a person's medical history can change the picture.

body.heading: What is a general anaesthetic?
body.body:
A general anaesthetic puts a person into a state of controlled unconsciousness, so they are asleep and feel nothing during the procedure.

A breathing tube is sometimes used, and it can cause a sore throat afterwards.

body.heading: How do I prepare?
body.body:
Hospitals ask people to follow fasting instructions before a general anaesthetic. Trusts give different timings, so the instructions from the hospital's own team apply.

Fasting matters because food or liquid left in the stomach could come back up to the back of the throat and be breathed into the lungs, causing injury. Trusts also give advice about dentures and alcohol beforehand, so the hospital's own instructions apply. Smoking makes a chest infection after an anaesthetic more likely.

One trust leaflet says that an operation will be cancelled on the day if the fasting rules were broken.

body.heading: What happens afterwards?
body.body:
After the anaesthetic wears off, common effects include sickness, feeling cold or shivering, and a sore throat. Medication may leave a person drowsy.

The effects of a general anaesthetic can last for around a day, and hospitals give aftercare advice.

body.heading: What are the risks?
body.body:
Anyone having a general anaesthetic is at some risk. Possible complications include a chest infection, particularly in people who smoke or have lung problems, and confusion, which is more common in older people and usually temporary.

Allergic reactions can be serious but are rare, and awareness during surgery is also rare. The anaesthetist discusses this before the operation.

heart-rhythm-monitors-holter-and-loop-re.name: Heart rhythm monitors: Holter and loop recorders
heart-rhythm-monitors-holter-and-loop-re.summary: A Holter monitor records the heart's electrical activity for 24 to 48 hours or longer, to catch rhythm problems that come and go. An implantable loop recorder can record for much longer.
keyPoints: A Holter (ambulatory ECG) monitor records the heart's electrical activity continuously, usually for about 24 to 48 hours and sometimes longer.
It can help find the cause of palpitations or diagnose conditions such as atrial fibrillation, which do not happen all the time.
The wearer keeps a diary of symptoms so that they can be matched against the recording, and returns the recorder to the hospital.
When shorter tests miss the problem, an implantable loop recorder placed under the skin of the chest can monitor for up to three years.

body.heading: Why would I need a heart rhythm monitor?
body.body:
An ordinary ECG records the heart for only a short time. The British Heart Foundation (BHF) describes a Holter monitor, also called an ambulatory ECG, as a way of recording the heart's electrical activity continuously over about 24 to 48 hours, sometimes longer.

It can help diagnose conditions such as atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm, or uncover the cause of palpitations that do not happen all the time.

body.heading: What is it like to wear a Holter monitor?
body.body:
Electrodes are stuck to the chest and their wires are taped down and connected to a small recorder. The person can carry on with most normal activities, but the monitor must be kept dry, so leaflets say not to bath or shower while it is worn.

A diary sheet is given to note the time and details of any symptoms so they can be matched against the recording. When the test is finished, the recorder is returned to the hospital so the results can be read.

body.heading: What if symptoms are rare?
body.body:
Some monitors, such as an event recorder, have a button the wearer presses when they have symptoms. Other devices can be worn for longer than a day or two.

A hospital leaflet describes an implantable loop recorder, which monitors the heart constantly, unlike an ECG or 24-hour monitor. This is a small device placed under the skin of the upper left chest, under local anaesthetic, that continuously monitors heart rate and rhythm and stores abnormal patterns. Recording can continue for up to three years, and the device only records, so it gives no shocks or treatment.

body.heading: How are symptoms recorded with a loop recorder?
body.body: Leaflets say the wearer presses an activator when they feel palpitations or dizziness, so the device saves the rhythm around that moment. Data is often sent to the healthcare team wirelessly through a home transmitter or smartphone app.

body.heading: Are these tests safe, and what about urgent symptoms?
body.body:
The BHF describes the Holter test as painless. An implantable loop recorder only monitors and records; it does not deliver shocks or other treatment.

The NHS advises calling 999 if palpitations come with chest pain, shortness of breath or feeling faint, and seeing a GP if they keep coming back or are worrying.

bone-marrow-biopsy-what-happens-and-why.name: Bone marrow biopsy: what happens and why
bone-marrow-biopsy-what-happens-and-why.summary: A bone marrow biopsy takes a small sample of marrow, usually from the back of the hip bone, to find out why blood counts are abnormal or to look for abnormal cells.
keyPoints: A bone marrow biopsy takes a small sample of bone marrow, usually from the back of the hip bone.
It is done to find out why blood counts are abnormal and to look for abnormal cells in the marrow.
Local anaesthetic numbs the area, and sedation may be offered; aching or bruising for a few days afterwards is common.
Results can take from a few days up to about four weeks, depending on the hospital and the tests, and are usually discussed at a clinic appointment.

body.heading: What is a bone marrow biopsy?
body.body:
Bone marrow is the spongy tissue inside bones where blood cells are made. A bone marrow biopsy removes a small sample so that it can be examined in a laboratory.

Macmillan says the sample is taken from the back of the hip bone, which is part of the pelvis, or occasionally from the breastbone. The test usually has two parts. An aspirate draws out liquid marrow with a syringe, and a trephine biopsy takes a small core of marrow using a slightly larger needle.

body.heading: Why might I need one?
body.body:
The test is usually done to work out why blood counts are abnormal and to look for abnormal cells. NHS leaflets list a low or high number of red cells, white cells or platelets, and infection, among the reasons.

The results help the doctor diagnose the illness and make decisions about care and treatment.

body.heading: What happens during the test?
body.body:
Local anaesthetic is used to numb the area, and gas and air may also be available. Medicine to help the person relax, called a sedative, may be offered.

It may feel uncomfortable for a few seconds while the liquid marrow is drawn into the syringe. A Macmillan booklet says the test takes about 20 to 30 minutes, though hospitals vary. One hospital leaflet says the whole appointment takes about an hour.

body.heading: What is it like afterwards?
body.body:
A dressing is placed over the area, and hospital leaflets say how long to keep it on and dry. After sedation, Macmillan advises not driving for 24 hours and having someone take the person home and stay with them overnight. Aching or a bruised feeling for a few days is common.

Hospital leaflets say patients are usually asked about blood-thinning medicines beforehand. Leaflets say to contact the hospital team about swelling or redness at the site; a GP or NHS 111 can also advise.

body.heading: What are the risks?
body.body:
Soreness and bruising at the site are common and usually last a few days. Serious complications are uncommon.

Bleeding at the site usually stops with pressure, sometimes leaving a small bruise. Infection and nerve injury are described as rare, and an allergic reaction to the numbing medicine is listed as a possible risk.

body.heading: When do results come back?
body.body: Timing varies by hospital. One trust says results can take up to two weeks, and another up to four weeks. Results are usually given at the next clinic appointment.
